messages.body_plain:
Again, sorry to have asked the same question twice, months apart. I got sidetracked on another project at the time, and when I returned to it, I had completely forgotten the earlier conversation. I got it working with this (snippet):

for(file.no <http://file.no> in 1:length(file.names)){
tryCatch(current<-scan(file.names[file.no <http://file.no>],what='char',quiet=T,quote='"',sep='\n'),warning=function(c){
c$message<-file.no <http://file.no>
problem.files<<-c(problem.files,as.numeric(c[1]))
} #close warning function
) #close tryCatch
} #next file.no <http://file.no>

Stefan, if you're still taking requests on what to include in the revision, a brief chapter on troubleshooting/debugging might come in handy. I found the ?tryCatch documentation pretty COIK (Clear Only If Known), and much of what I found on the web on it assumes you know similar processes in other languages.

messages.body_plain:
All,

Before I start downloading data I was interested
in the best format to save the data.

I plan on analysing the files using the R package TM.

Below is how the data looks like when downloaded.
I anticipate about 50 such data files. Is it
better to put all the data in one file or one
file per article, in a single folder?  if a
single file, is there any recommended method to
separate articles or are the headers sufficient?

I'm interested in looking at frequently used
words and word co-occurrence. The analysis is
part of a presentation I want to do and not part of any academic study.

Any assistance is appreciated,

Bob

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Data file format for analysis using TM
messages.subject_clean: [CorpLing with R] Data file format for analysis using TM
messages.body_plain:
Bob,

It looks to me you have a small data munging project ahead of you ;) Stefan certainly has more insight, but I'd think you want to make a standard "dataset" out of all these files. They can remain separate files, but there needs to be a process to read one in, and tidy it up in sense hadly wickham's "tidy data": http://vita.had.co.nz/papers/tidy-data.pdf. After that's done, you can bind it all together.

In other words, the ideal would be to end up with a data.frame where each row is a single observation coming from a single file. So the columns of this data.frame would be SE, HD, AU, etc. Here's a skeleton piece of code that I use often to read in all files in a directory and bind them together.

library('plyr')  # for rbind.fill

readDataDF <- function(fname, ...){
  # Read in a single data file and perform munging, probably starting with
  # readLines in your case, Bob, since the data are not in a table format.
  # Extract things from fname and add in as extra columns if needed.
  return(dat)  # return a tidy data.frame for a single file.
}

# Read in flags.
text_files <- list.files(path=file.path("data", "docs"), full.names=T)
corpus <- rbind.fill(lapply (text_files, readDataDF))

# Write out the data.
write.csv(corpus, file=file.path("data", "processed", "corpus.csv"),
          row.names=FALSE)

A more generic version of this file can be found here: https://gist.github.com/boethian/c02e61e92c82a091dffd

Now, I'm unfamiliar with the tm package and it seems to have its own document management system, but it seems like it would be a lot more work to get it to understand your documents, than to clean up your own documents into a standard form, which could then be written to a CSV as above (which the vignette says it can take in as well: http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/tm/vignettes/tm.pdf).

If the the readDataDF function above becomes too unwieldy, you may need to pop it out to do more surgical work on each file. What comes to mind to me is to reading that file as if it were already a data.frame using read.table (with a "\t" sep, it looks like), but clearly each row is actually a column, and presumably the file name could contain what could form the "key" / row name identifier. So I would read in a file, then make it into a wide format with R package reshape2, so that the rows become columns. Then you should be good to go.

Despite being on this list, I'm unsure if there are other text processing / corpus linguistic packages that would help here, but this would be my approach with more general R tools.

Alex
